questions.q: What does "accuracy" measure as a data quality dimension?
options: How closely a value reflects the real-world fact it represents
Whether a value matches an expected format or data type
Whether a value is missing or present
Whether a value is duplicated elsewhere in the table
questions.explain: Accuracy is about truth — whether the stored value matches reality — not about format or presence, which are other dimensions (validity and completeness).

questions.q: A phone number column contains the value 555-0199, correctly formatted as a US phone number, but it does not actually reach the customer it's assigned to. What is this an example of?
options: Valid but inaccurate data
Invalid and inaccurate data
Valid and accurate data
Incomplete data
questions.explain: It's correctly formatted (valid) but doesn't reflect the real-world fact (inaccurate) — the exact distinction between validity and accuracy.

questions.q: Why can't an accuracy check be performed with a rule applied to a single table alone?
options: Accuracy requires comparison against a trusted external reference, not just an internal rule
SQL cannot evaluate WHERE clauses against a single table
Accuracy only applies to numeric columns
Accuracy checks must always run outside the database
questions.explain: Because accuracy is about matching real-world truth, you need a trusted comparison point — a system of record, reference table, or external verification — not just an internal format rule.

questions.q: In the sample-based accuracy query, what does aggregating the mismatch count across an audited sample produce?
options: An estimated accuracy rate for the whole table
A list of every duplicate row in the table
A count of NULL values in the table
A referential integrity violation report
questions.explain: When a full reference table isn't available, comparing a smaller audited sample against the target and aggregating mismatches yields a trackable estimated accuracy rate.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a common cause of inaccurate data?
options: The column's data type being too short for the value
Manual entry errors like transposed digits
Stale source data that hasn't been updated after a real-world change
Integration mapping bugs during an ETL load
questions.explain: A too-short data type would cause a validity/format problem (truncation or rejection), not an accuracy problem. The lesson's listed causes were manual entry errors, stale data, mapping bugs, and unit/currency mismatches.
